notes: The whole 189-page adopted PDF, read end to end: the preface, contributors and introduction; the historic context chapters (Late, Post & New: Architectural Modernism & Its Discontents; changes within professional practice and education; architectural criticism, publications and exhibitions; San Francisco in the late twentieth century; redevelopment, anti-Manhattanization and urban planning; the public realm, waterfront, POPOS and public art; the historic preservation movement and adaptive reuse; the environmental movement and hippie Modernism; the live/work ordinance; late twentieth century landscape architecture); the three themes -- Late Modernism, Postmodernism and New Modernism -- and the four sub-themes -- Corporate Late Modernism, Brutalism, New Formalism and the Third Bay Tradition -- with their narratives, evaluation criteria, eligibility standards, character-defining features and integrity considerations; all 190 figures; the bibliography; and Appendices A (architects and designers identified in research, and demographic shifts in local professional practice), B (a shortlist of 65 representative sites built 1970-2000) and C (a 1960-2000 timeline). There is no inventory table and no APN anywhere in the document. Appendix B is the closest thing to one and it is the batch's densest page: 65 entries, nearly all with an address, a year and an architect.

Repeated mentions of one address were folded into a single finding except where the statement records a second dated fact about the same parcel: 555 California Street carries three (the tower, A.P. Giannini Plaza and the Nagare sculpture), 600 Montgomery Street two (the Pyramid and Redwood Park), 2 Folsom Street two (the tower and its POPOS), and 1111 8th Street two (the 1951 bus garage and its 1998 conversion). Nearly every address carries an architect, a firm or a year, which is what makes a statement with no inventory this dense: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, William Pereira, John Portman, Welton Becket, Hertzka & Knowles, John Carl Warnecke, Johnson & Burgee, Paffard Keatinge-Clay, Daniel Solomon, Donald MacDonald, Jeremy Kotas, Beverly Willis, Tanner Leddy Maytum Stacy, Stanley Saitowitz, Jim Jennings, Backen Arrigoni & Ross, Fisher-Friedman, EHDD, Kotas/Pantaleoni, Levy Art + Architecture, Gary Gee, Millard Sheets, T.Y. Lin, Lawrence Halprin, Barbara Stauffacher Solomon and Mai Arbegast among them. Buildings the statement names with no street number, and so not recorded as findings: the Buchanan Street Park and Buchanan Pedestrian Mall, Hilltop Park, Sydney Walton Park, Yerba Buena Gardens, Crissy Field, the Ferry Building, Harry Bridges Plaza, Pier 39, Victorian Mews (given only as a block), the 16th and 24th Street Mission BART stations, Glen Park and Balboa Park BART stations, the Japanese Cultural & Trade Center, the Palace of the Legion of Honor, the Market Street cultural landscape and the 18th & Arkansas lofts. Two addresses were seen and deliberately not recorded under the people rule, because the only fact attached to each is who lived there: 1218 Montgomery Street and 500 Capp Street. Addresses outside San Francisco (550 Madison Avenue and 1083 Fifth Avenue in New York, Ronchamp, Philadelphia, The Sea Ranch, Orinda) were not recorded.
